_about: The sacrifice hub (plan 7.6f), built as the other hubs are: the rows are defined by the Hebrew and Greek words standing in the verse (a noun row by the words in the noun's own verse, a verb row by who sacrifices and to whom), by hand where the text's own phrase is what makes the row (pick), and a verse sits in every row it fits (match: all). The words are the card's own: the Hebrew זֶבַח and זָבַח (sacrifice) and עֹלָה (burnt offering), their Aramaic counterparts (Ezra), and the Greek θυσία, θύω, ὁλοκαύτωμα, προσφορά, προσφέρω, ἀναφέρω and εἰδωλόθυτος. The Hebrew words for the other kinds of offering (מִנְחָה grain offering or gift, חַטָּאת sin offering, אָשָׁם guilt offering, שֶׁלֶם peace offering, קׇרְבָּן, אִשֶּׁה) are different words that the English also calls offering; they are named apart under 'Other words', each with its verses, and are used in the rows only as companion words that stand in the same verse as one of the card's own. The rows of each form are in the Bible's order of the earliest verse each holds (the catch-all last), so that no order suggests that one thing a sacrifice does outranks another. The three contested points of this page (what a sacrifice does; whether the sacrifices of the law are fulfilled, ended or continued; the Lord's Supper) are set out as rows of the text's own words, each with a note that the page takes no side. Built by tools/concepts/hub_build.py into out/concept-hubs/sacrifice.json.

titles.noun: What the text says of sacrifice
titles.verb: Who sacrifices, to whom, and where

_words_why: The card's own three Hebrew words (זֶבַח, זָבַח, עֹלָה) with the Greek that renders them (θυσία and θύω for זבח; ὁλοκαύτωμα for עלה, Mark 12:33 and Heb 10:6, 8), the Aramaic of Ezra (דְּבַח, עַלְוָה), and the New Testament's other words for offering a sacrifice: προσφορά 'offering' (Heb 10:10, 14, 18; Eph 5:2; Acts 21:26), προσφέρω 'offer' (Heb 5-10; Matt 5:23-24; 8:4) and ἀναφέρω 'offer up' (Heb 7:27; 13:15; Jas 2:21; 1 Pet 2:5), without which Heb 9:14 and 9:28 would not be on the page, and εἰδωλόθυτος 'food sacrificed to idols' (1 Cor 8; Acts 15:29; Rev 2:14, 20), set with the nouns. The hub never says the Hebrew and the Greek are one word: every example names the word it stands on. The card lists no Greek word of its own; these were added because the New Testament's sacrifice verses cannot be reached otherwise.
_sense_why: Measured on MACULA's gloss in each verse (2026-10-25, build 1). זבח: 'sacrific-' in all but ten verses; the ten are Deut 12:15 and 12:21 ('you will slaughter', meat for eating, not an offering), 2 Kgs 23:20 ('he slaughtered' the priests of the high places), Ezek 34:3 ('you slaughter' the fattened animals) and a few more, and drop out as another sense. 2 Chr 18:2 ('Ahab sacrificed many sheep and cattle for him') is glossed 'slaughtered' but the Berean prints 'sacrificed': put back by sense_keep. θύω: 6 of 13 (the rest are 'kill': Matt 22:4, Luke 15:23, John 10:10, Acts 10:13). προσφέρω: 28 of 44 (the rest are 'bring', 'present': bringing the sick and the children to Jesus). ἀναφέρω: 4 of 9 ('bear', 'carry up': 1 Pet 2:24). Matt 2:11 (the magi 'offered gifts'), Luke 23:36 (the soldiers 'offering' wine) and Acts 8:18 (Simon 'offered' money) pass the gloss rule and are not sacrifice: sense_drop.

sense_keep.2Chr.18.2: Ahab sacrificed many sheep and cattle (a feast for Jehoshaphat): the Berean prints 'sacrificed'; MACULA's gloss is 'slaughtered'

Matt.2.11.why: the magi 'offered gifts' to the child: προσφέρω is 'present' here, no sacrifice

Luke.23.36.why: the soldiers 'offering' Him sour wine: προσφέρω is 'bring to', no sacrifice

Acts.8.18.why: Simon 'offered' the apostles money: προσφέρω is 'bring to', no sacrifice

others._why: Words the English also calls sacrifice or offering, named apart as love names φιλέω and חֶסֶד apart: a different word is never handed over as the same. מִנְחָה is gift, tribute or grain offering (Abel's and Cain's offerings, Gen 4:3-5, are this word, not זֶבַח); חַטָּאת is 'sin' and 'sin offering', one word; אָשָׁם 'guilt offering'; שֶׁלֶם 'peace offering'; עָלָה is the verb 'go up' that goes with the burnt offering. עָשָׂה 'do, make' (h6213) is excluded: the Berean prints 'offer' where the phrase is 'make a burnt offering', and the word is 'do'. 'add' puts first the verses that show each word best.
others.title: Other words translated “sacrifice” and “offering”

h4503.note: מִנְחָה means a gift, tribute or grain offering. Cain's and Abel's offerings (Gen 4:3-5) are this word; the word for sacrifice, זֶבַח, is not used there. Heb 11:4 calls Abel's offering a θυσία, a sacrifice.

h2403.note: חַטָּאת is one Hebrew word for 'sin' and for the 'sin offering'; the Berean prints 'sin offering' where the verse is about the offering. It is a different word from זֶבַח.

h817.note: אָשָׁם is the 'guilt offering' (and 'guilt'); a different word from זֶבַח.

h8002.note: שֶׁלֶם (plural שְׁלָמִים) is the 'peace offering', a kind of זֶבַח in Lev 3 and 7; it is a different word.

h5927.note: עָלָה is the verb 'go up'; the Berean prints 'offered up' where the thing that goes up is the burnt offering. The noun עֹלָה is one of the hub's own words.

See the worker report.

rows.label: A pleasing aroma; a fragrant offering
rows.note: The text's own phrase: “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” in the laws of Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers, the first time at Gen 8:21 after Noah's burnt offerings, and taken up at Eph 5:2 and Phil 4:18 (“a fragrant offering”). What the aroma means -- the LORD's pleasure, His acceptance of the worshiper, His anger turned away -- readers take differently, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the rule on the Hebrew נִיחֹחַ and the Greek ὀσμή gave these 24 verses; Gen 8:21 is added because it is the verse that says the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma and has no word for sacrifice itself (Gen 8:20, the sacrifice, stands in the catch-all). A rule row cannot take a verse with none of the hub's words.

rows.label: Isaac: “offer him as a burnt offering”, “the lamb for the burnt offering”
rows.note: Genesis 22 as the verses have it: the word to Abraham to offer Isaac as a burnt offering, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering”, and the ram offered “in place of his son”. Heb 11:17 and Jas 2:21 take it up, the second inside an argument about faith and works (see the faith page). Readers part on what the story shows -- a test of Abraham, a substitute provided, a picture of a later sacrifice -- and the page takes no side. The children given to other gods are the row further down.
rows._why: by hand: Isaac is named in every verse; the Hebrew verse 22:9-10 has no sacrifice word so is not here. Heb 11:17 and Jas 2:21 are verb-form verses (προσφέρω, ἀναφέρω) set in a noun row because the argument is one.

rows.label: Bull, ram, lamb, goat, dove; “without blemish”

not_verses.Ezek.40.38: אֵילִם is the gateway's 'porticoes'; MACULA's lemma is אַיִל 'ram', but the verse has no animal

rows._why: what was brought. Merged (2026-10-25) from two rows, the animals and 'without blemish' (22 verses), to hold the page to its size: a verse that names an animal and one that names the defect are both about what the offerer brought.

rows.label: Eating from the sacrifice

not_verses.Lev.6.10: אָכַל here is the fire 'consuming' the burnt offering on the altar, not eating
not_verses.Lev.9.24: the fire from the LORD 'consumed' the burnt offering: it is the LORD's fire, no one eats
not_verses.1Kgs.18.38: the fire of the LORD 'consumed' the burnt offering: not eating
not_verses.2Chr.7.1: fire from heaven 'consumed' the burnt offering: not eating
not_verses.Jer.46.10: the sword 'devours' in the day of the LORD's sacrifice: a figure of slaughter, not a meal

rows.note: Where worshipers, priests or guests eat of a sacrifice (Gen 31:54; Lev 7:15; Deut 12:27), and where the New Testament speaks of eating food sacrificed to idols (1 Cor 8:10; Rev 2:14) and of “those who eat the sacrifices” as “fellow partakers in the altar” (1 Cor 10:18). What the shared meal means -- fellowship with the LORD, a gift received from Him, a sharing in what is offered -- readers take differently, and the page takes no side. The LORD's own “sacrificial feast” for the birds and beasts is here too (Ezek 39:17-19). The fire that consumes a sacrifice is not here; it is under “Every other use”.
rows._why: by rule on אָכַל and ἐσθίω (which take every verse with 'eat'), minus five verses where אָכַל is the fire or the sword consuming, each with its reason.

rows.label: The Passover
rows.note: The text calls it a sacrifice (Exod 12:27; 34:25; Deut 16:2), names the day “when the Passover lamb was sacrificed” (Mark 14:12; Luke 22:7), and Paul writes “Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed” (1 Cor 5:7). How the Passover and the death of Christ are related, readers take differently; the page sets the verses side by side and takes no side.
rows._why: by hand, so the New Testament verses (verb-form: θύω) stand with the Hebrew ones; a rule on פֶּסַח gave only the four Hebrew noun-form verses (Exod 12:27, 34:25, 2 Chr 30:15, 35:16).

rows.label: Peace offering, thank offering, vow, freewill offering
rows._why: the kinds of sacrifice that were shared and eaten, named by the Hebrew words that stand in the verse; used as companion words, since they are not the card's own.

rows.label: Blood beside sacrifice
rows.note: Blood is named in the same verse as the sacrifice: put on the altar (Lev 4:7), sprinkled (Ezek 43:18), not to be offered with leaven (Exod 23:18), and in the Council's letter forbidden to eat (Acts 15:29). The prophets also picture a day of judgment as the LORD's own sacrifice, “bathed in blood” (Isa 34:6; Jer 46:10; Ezek 39:17-19). What the blood does -- covers, cleanses, ransoms, gives a life for a life -- readers take differently, and the page takes no side. Lev 17:11 and Heb 9:22, which have no word for sacrifice, are among the verses at the head of the page.
rows._why: by rule on דָּם and αἷμα, in the verse. Luke 13:1 ('whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices') shows the label as written.

rows.label: Daily, Sabbath, New Moon and festival offerings

not_verses.Ps.50.8: תָּמִיד here is 'ever before Me': the burnt offerings are always before the LORD, not the daily offering

rows._add_why: 'the appointed feasts' (מוֹעֵד): Lev 23:37 and Num 15:3 name the festival offerings by that word, which cannot be a rule word because it is also the 'Tent of Meeting'
rows._why: by rule; מוֹעֵד left out of the words (it is 'appointed time' and also the 'Tent of Meeting', Lev 1:3 and 4:7 were in the row for the tent); חֹדֶשׁ is 'new moon' and 'month', both in Num 28-29.

rows.label: Atonement made; a hand laid on the head
rows.note: The text says the priest “will make atonement” for the offerer with the offering, and in Lev 4:26 and 5:10 “he will be forgiven”; it says the offerer “lays his hand on the head” of the offering (Lev 1:4; 4:24). What atonement does -- covers, cleanses, ransoms, turns away wrath -- and what the hand laid on the head does -- identifies, dedicates, transfers -- readers take differently, and the page takes no side. The Hebrew is כִּפֶּר, a different word from the one for forgive (see forgiveness, where the two are set side by side). The sin offering of Lev 4-5 is also under “Sacrifice and sin”, below.
rows._why: by rule; merged (2026-10-25) with the hand laid on the head (6 verses), which is the gesture of the same offerings (Lev 1:4 has both).

rows.label: Sacrifice and sin: the sin offering, the guilt offering, “for sins”
rows._add_why: 2026-10-25 review: the note names Heb 10:18 (προσφορά, 'an offering for sin is no longer needed') and 10:26 (θυσία, 'no further sacrifice for sins remains'); both were already in the row by the rule on ἁμαρτία (built row: 62 before and after); named here so they stay if the rule changes
rows.note: In Hebrew חַטָּאת is both 'sin' and 'sin offering'; the Berean prints 'sin offering' where the verse is about the offering, and the verse reads 'sins' where it is not (Isa 43:24; Hos 8:13). Heb 10:26 (“no further sacrifice for sins remains”) stands here with Heb 10:12 and 10:18; where Christian traditions part on whether a believer can fall away, and on what Heb 10:26 says of it, the page takes no side. The sin offering's ritual in Lev 4-5 is also in the row “Atonement made; a hand laid on the head”, above.
rows._why: by rule on the companion words; Heb 10:26 is a hard verse and stays. 16-verse check, build 3: Isa 43:24 ('you have not satisfied Me with the fat of your sacrifices ... burdened Me with your sins') is not 'sacrifice for sin', so the label was 'Sacrifice for sin: ...' and failed; relabelled 'Sacrifice and sin' (the verse names both) rather than hide a hard verse.

rows.label: Sacrifice set beside what the LORD asks: not desired, not accepted, “mercy, not sacrifice”
rows.note: Set side by side as the text has them: “obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Sam 15:22), “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire” (Ps 40:6; Heb 10:5, 8), “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hos 6:6; Matt 9:13; 12:7), and the sacrifices He does not accept (Isa 1:11; Jer 6:20; 14:12; Amos 5:22; Hos 8:13). Readers part on whether these verses set the sacrifices of the law aside, or reject only a sacrifice offered without mercy, justice and obedience; and on how Ps 40:6 (“my ears You have opened”) stands to Heb 10:5 (“a body You prepared for Me”), which the Berean prints differently. In Jer 7:22 the Berean reads “did not merely command them”; the Hebrew has no word for “merely”. Amos 5:25 (“Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness?”), quoted at Acts 7:42, is a question and stands under “Every other use”; readers part on what answer it expects. The page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the verses where the LORD says He does not desire or accept sacrifice, or sets mercy, justice or obedience beside it. Mic 6:8, Amos 5:24 and Isa 1:13 are in the speeches whose other verses are here (Mic 6:6-8; Amos 5:21-25; Isa 1:11-17) and have no sacrifice word themselves; Mic 6:8 and Amos 5:24 are tied to the sacrifice card in the graph (the texts 'what does the LORD require of you' and 'let justice roll on like a river'). Merged from three rows (2026-10-25): 'not desired' (Ps 40:6; Heb 10), 'mercy not sacrifice', and 'will not accept'. Ps 50:8 ('I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices') is the other side and is in the catch-all. 16-verse check, build 3: Amos 5:25 (a question) did not show 'not desired, not accepted' and was taken out with Mic 6:7 (also only a question, no word of the card's own); the label became 'set beside what the LORD asks', which Mic 6:6 with 6:8 and Jer 7:22 with 7:23 show. Jer 7:22: the Hebrew words of the verse were read in MACULA (not-spoke with your fathers, not-commanded them, on the day of bringing them out of Egypt, concerning burnt offering and sacrifice); there is no word for 'merely'. A finding for ontology/translation-findings.json.

rows.label: A son or daughter given in sacrifice
rows.note: The text records it as the act of the king of Moab (2 Kgs 3:27), as Israel's sin (Ps 106:37-38; Ezek 16:20; Hos 13:2 says “They offer human sacrifice”, in the verb row for other gods) and as the worship of Baal, “something I never commanded or mentioned, nor did it even enter My mind” (Jer 19:5). Isaac, whom the LORD tells Abraham to offer, is the row above. Jephthah's vow (Judg 11:31), “I will offer it up as a burnt offering”, is under “Every other use: sacrifice, offering”; that verse says only “whatever comes out of the door”, and says nothing of approval.
rows._why: by hand: each verse names sons, daughters or a firstborn given as an offering. Judg 11:31 (Jephthah's vow) says only 'whatever comes out of the door' and is not here. Hard verses stay.

rows.label: Other gods, idols and demons
rows.note: Verses where a sacrifice is named beside another god, an idol or a demon: Naaman's vow (2 Kgs 5:17), Jehu's sacrifice to Baal (2 Kgs 10:19), the golden calf (Acts 7:41), Paul on food sacrificed to idols (1 Cor 8; 10:19), the Council's letter (Acts 15:29) and the letters to Pergamum and Thyatira (Rev 2:14, 20). The verbs are in the next form, under “Other gods, idols and demons”.
rows._why: by rule on the companion words. One lemma, אַחֵר, is 'other' also in 'another', so every example was read.

rows.label: Thanksgiving, praise, a broken spirit, bodies and lives as sacrifices
rows.note: Sacrifices that are not animals: a thank offering (Ps 50:14), “the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit” (Ps 51:17), “living sacrifices” (Rom 12:1), “a sacrifice of praise” (Heb 13:15), “spiritual sacrifices” (1 Pet 2:5), gifts as “a fragrant offering” (Phil 4:18), and the apostle “poured out like a drink offering” (Phil 2:17; 2 Tim 4:6). Readers part on whether these replace the offerings of the law or stand beside them; the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand. 2 Tim 4:6 has no sacrifice word (σπένδω 'poured out as a drink offering', which the card ties to this theme, the sacrifice and service of your faith). 2 Chr 33:16 and Ps 50:14, 23 are literal thank offerings and stand with the rest on the word 'thank'.

rows.label: Sacrifice in days to come: offered, or absent
rows.note: The text sets both beside each other: burnt offerings and sacrifices “accepted on My altar” (Isa 56:7), the Egyptians worshiping “with sacrifices and offerings” (Isa 19:21), “then bulls will be offered on Your altar” (Ps 51:19), priests who will “never fail to have a man ... to offer burnt offerings” (Jer 33:18), the sacrifices at the temple Ezekiel is shown (Ezek 40-46: 40:39; 43:18, 27; 44:11; 45:17; 46:2, 24 here), all who sacrifice coming to cook in the pots of Jerusalem (Zech 14:21); and, on the other side, Israel “many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or sacred pillar” (Hos 3:4; 3:5 goes on to their return), and one who “will put an end to sacrifice and offering” (Dan 9:27). Ps 51:19 comes after a prayer for Zion's walls (51:18), “then” bulls will be offered. Readers part on whether these are sacrifices still to be offered, pictures of worship in the new covenant, or already fulfilled; on who “he” is in Dan 9:27 and when; and on how Heb 10:18 (“an offering for sin is no longer needed”) stands to them. The page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the verses in which the prophets say what will become of sacrifice. Ezek 40-46 has 30-odd verses with the hub's words; seven that show different things (a place to slaughter, the altar's rules, the LORD's acceptance, the ministers, the prince's part, the kitchens) stand here and the rest are in the rows by their words. Zech 14:21 is a verb-form verse (זבח) without a frame in the graph, so no rule reaches it. Mal 1:11 and Isa 66:20 have no word of the card's own.

rows.label: The Lord's table: “This is My body”, blood “poured out”, “in remembrance of Me”, “a participation”
rows.note: The words of the Last Supper and Paul on the table: “Take and eat; this is My body” (Matt 26:26; Mark 14:22), “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt 26:28; Mark 14:24 has “which is poured out for many”), “do this in remembrance of Me” (Luke 22:19; 1 Cor 11:24-25), “a participation in the blood of Christ” (1 Cor 10:16), “those who eat the sacrifices ... fellow partakers in the altar” (1 Cor 10:18), “the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Cor 10:21). Only 1 Cor 10:18 has a word for sacrifice; the others are here because they speak of the body, the blood, the covenant and the meal. The covenant sealed with burnt and peace offerings and “the blood of the covenant” is at Exod 24:5-8 (Exod 24:5 is under “Sacrificed to the LORD”, in the verb form). The other words of the tellings of the Supper (Matt 26:27; 1 Cor 11:23, 26) are not set here, having no word for sacrifice. Readers part on whether the Lord's Supper is itself a sacrifice, a memorial, a participation in Christ's body and blood, or more than one of these; the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand, the one place on the page where verses are set without a word of the card: the owner's contested list names 'the Lord's Supper as sacrifice or memorial', and the card's graph holds event_last_supper as a core concept of this card (Matt 26:28; Luke 22:20). Mark 14:22-24, Matt 26:26-27 and 1 Cor 11:23, 26 tell the same Supper and Heb 13:10 ('We have an altar') has no word of the card's: widening the row with them is HELD for the editor (2026-10-25 review: the Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran seats asked for it; the secular scholar and the literary teacher asked that verses with no sacrifice word not be added). The note now says only that these verses speak of blood, covenant and the meal, and points to Exod 24:5-8.

rows.label: Hebrews: offered again and again, unable to cleanse; once for all
rows.note: Hebrews on the sacrifices of the law and the sacrifice of Christ: “the same sacrifices offered year after year” (10:1), “again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins” (10:11), “gifts and sacrifices being offered were unable to cleanse the conscience” (9:9); and “once for all ... by the sacrifice of Himself” (9:26), “the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (10:10), “one sacrifice for sins” (10:12), “a single offering” (10:14). Heb 9:26 names Christ, and 10:10 Jesus Christ; 7:27, 10:12 and 10:14 say “He” or “this Priest” inside the same argument. Readers part on whether the sacrifices of the law are fulfilled in Christ's, ended by it, or continue in some form, and on how “once for all” stands to the Lord's table; the page takes no side. The rows above say what the law's offerings were given for, for example the priest “will make atonement for that man's sin, and he will be forgiven” (Lev 4:26); the page says nothing on how that stands to Heb 9:9 or 10:1.
rows._why: by hand: the two sets of Hebrews verses that the text itself contrasts, in one row so that neither reads as the answer to the other. Heb 7:27 has both ('daily sacrifices' and 'once for all').

rows.label: Every other use: sacrifice, offering
rows.note: Among them: Noah's burnt offerings after the flood (Gen 8:20); the fire from the LORD that consumed the offering (Lev 9:24; 1 Kgs 18:38; 2 Chr 7:1); the dedications, of the altar (“the dedication offering for the altar after it was anointed”, Num 7:88) and of the house (“the king and all the Israelites dedicated the house of the LORD”, 1 Kgs 8:63; “the king and all the people dedicated the house of God”, 2 Chr 7:5; see also 2 Chr 7); Abel's sacrifice (Heb 11:4); Ps 50:8 (“I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices”); and Amos 5:25 with Acts 7:42, the question “Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness?”

rows.label: Sacrificed to the LORD, before the LORD
rows._why: by hand, from the rule on the LORD in the verb's own clause (34 verses) with the verses added whose verb has no frame in the graph or whose clause names God or the Lord: Exod 5:8 and 8:25 ('sacrifice to our God', 'sacrifice to your God'), 1 Sam 6:15, Gen 46:1 (the God of his father Isaac), Mal 1:14 (sacrificing a defective animal 'to the Lord'). Deut 16:5-6 are in the Passover row, not here: they name the place, not the one sacrificed to. Zech 14:21 is in 'days to come'. Exodus asks again and again to 'sacrifice to the LORD' in the wilderness (3:18; 5:3, 8, 17; 8:8, 25-29).

rows.label: Other gods, idols and demons
rows.note: Exod 22:20 and 2 Kgs 17:35 forbid it; the others record it: the golden calf (Exod 32:8), the goat demons (Lev 17:7), the calves at Bethel (1 Kgs 12:32), Dagon (Judg 16:23), the gods of Damascus (2 Chr 28:23), the Baals (Hos 11:2), Zeus (Acts 14:13), and “the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God” (1 Cor 10:20).
rows._why: by hand. The rule on the idol words (build 1) found 8 verbs (Exod 32:8, Deut 32:17, 2 Kgs 17:35, 2 Chr 33:22, Ps 106:37-38, Hos 11:2, 1 Cor 10:20); Exod 22:20, 2 Chr 34:4 and Hos 13:2 have no frame in the graph, so no rule reaches them; Exod 34:15, Lev 17:7, Judg 16:23, 1 Kgs 11:8, 12:32, 2 Chr 28:23 and Acts 14:13, 18 were in the catch-all and are read: each names the other god, the calves, Dagon, the gods of Damascus or Zeus. Hos 4:13-14 (sacrifice on the mountaintops, with shrine prostitutes) and Hab 1:16 (sacrifices to his dragnet) name no other god and are left out; Hos 4:13 is in the high-places row.

rows.label: At the high places, on the hills, under the trees
rows._add_why: the same sacrifice 'on the mountaintops ... on the hills, under oak' (Hos 4:13), 'a high and lofty mountain' (Isa 57:7), 'every high hill or leafy tree' (Ezek 20:28), where the Hebrew has the hill and not the word בָּמָה
rows.note: 1 Kgs 3:2 gives a reason (“because a house had not yet been built for the name of the LORD”); 2 Chr 33:17 says the people “still sacrificed on the high places, but only to the LORD their God”; the kings of Judah who did right are told, “the high places were not removed” (1 Kgs 22:43; 2 Kgs 12:3; 14:4; 15:4, 35); 1 Kgs 12:32 and 13:2 are Jeroboam's altar and the word against it.

rows.label: The gift offered at the altar and by the priest, “according to the law”
rows.note: The Gospels, Acts and Hebrews speak of offerings made under the law: “if you are offering your gift at the altar” (Matt 5:23-24), “offer the gift that Moses commanded” (Matt 8:4; Mark 1:44; Luke 5:14), “until the offering for each of them was made” (Acts 21:26), priests “who offer gifts according to the law” (Heb 8:4) and the high priest who offers for himself and for the people (Heb 5:1, 3; 9:7). Readers part on whether these sacrifices are fulfilled, ended or continue; the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: προσφέρω in the sense of the gift offered at the altar. The verses in which Hebrews contrasts the priest's offering with Christ's are in 'Christ offered himself' and in the noun row 'Year after year ... once for all'.

rows.label: Christ offered Himself; Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed
rows.note: Heb 9:14 (“the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God”), 9:28 (“Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many”) and 1 Cor 5:7 name Christ; Heb 7:27, 9:25 and 10:12 say “He”, “Himself” or “this Priest” in the argument of the same letter, where Jesus is named (7:24; 10:10). What this sacrifice does -- atones, redeems, substitutes, conquers, shows God's love -- readers take differently, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand, as the divine persons are: the verbs of the New Testament's sacrifice of Christ (θύω, προσφέρω, ἀναφέρω). Each verse is read; Eph 5:2 and Heb 9:26, 10:10 are noun-form verses in the noun rows.

rows.label: Every other use: sacrificed, offered
rows.note: Among them: the verb of sacrifice said of something that is not an animal, “offered up prayers and petitions” (Heb 5:7) and “offering service to God” (John 16:2); and David's and Solomon's sacrifices at the ark and the temple (2 Sam 6:13; 1 Kgs 8:5). Abraham offering Isaac (Heb 11:17; Jas 2:21) is also here in the verb, and is set in the Isaac row of the first form.
